## Problem 1

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(ggridges)
library(patchwork)

data("ny_noaa")
```

In the dataset ny_noaa, there are 2,595,176 rows and 7 columns. Key variables are id, date, prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, and tmin. From the first 10 rows shown in the console, there are NA values for every variable except for id and date. I believe that missing data is a great issue in this dataset.

```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
    prcp = as.numeric(prcp)/10
  )

ny_noaa |> 
  group_by(snow) |> 
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)
```

The most commonly observed snowfall is 0 mm, and that is because snowfall is during the winter, and winter makes up about 1/4 of a year. 

### Two-panel plot with average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years

```{r}
ny_noaa |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1,7)) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
    summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>  
  mutate(
    month_name = case_match(
      month,
      1 ~ "January",
      7 ~ "July"
    )
  )|> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, color = id)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month_name) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The average maximum temperatures are lower in January than in July, across the years. This makes sense because January is one of the coldest months in the year and July is one of the hottest. There are several outliers in the January scatterplot (range: -17 C to 13 C) and fewer outliers in the July one (< 15 C).

### Two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset and (ii) the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year

```{r}
temp_diff = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmax, y = tmin)) +
  geom_hex() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

snowfall_year = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

(temp_diff/snowfall_year)
```

## Problem 2

### Load, tidy, merge, and organize the data sets

```{r}
accel_df =
  read_csv("nhanes_accel.csv", 
           na = c("NA","", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "min",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  )

covar_df =
  read_csv("nhanes_covar.csv",
           na = c("NA","","."),
           skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "male",
      2 ~ "female"
    ),
    sex = factor(sex),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "less than high school",
      2 ~ "high school equivalent",
      3 ~ "more than high school"
    ),
  education = factor(
    education, levels = c("less than high school", "high school equivalent", "more than high school"))
  )

accel_final =
  left_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn") |> 
  filter(age >= 21)
```

### Number of men and women in each education category; visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category

```{r}
accel_final |> 
  group_by(sex) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

accel_final |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education)
```

* In the dataset, there is 158,400 women (females) and 169,920 men (males)
* In the boxplot, the median age between men and women who's education level is less than high school are the most similar (around 60 years old), while the median for both sexes who's education level is high school equivalent is the most different (62 years for women, 53 years for men). Women and men who's education level is more than high school have the lowest median compared to the other education level groups, with ages 41 and 43, respectfully.

### Plot: total activities vs age by education level and sex

```{r}
accel_final |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

* In all three education level plots, the common trend is that as one increases in age, their total activity decreases (negative relationship). 
* The high school equivalent and more than high school plots show that females have an overall higher total activity than males, whereas in the less than high school plot, men have the higher total activity after age 40.
* The more than high school plot, there is more variability in the graph compared to the other education levels.

### Three-panel plot: 24-hour activity time courses vs hour by education level and sex

```{r}
accel_final |> 
  mutate(min = as.numeric(min)) |> 
  group_by(min, sex, education) |> 
  summarize(
    daily_activity_time = mean(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
    ) |> 
  mutate(hour = min/60) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = daily_activity_time, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

* In all three education plots, the 24-day activity time peaked around the 10th hour, slightly plateaued until the 20th hour, and then decreased. Overall, females have a higher activity time compared to males across all education levels. Less than high school had the highest 24-day activity time at almost 16 g-mins.
